evidence.text: It's just one of my things, as an investor. I want to see something working. I want to know that you can build something that's actually functional. So I'm going to pass right now.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: All right, well I'm going to get started here. I'm Anthony with Force Impact Technologies.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Force impact.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Force Impact Technologies. And we've created the FIT Platform. Our goal was to identify, document and reduce the amount of traumatic brain injuries in sports. Ever since I was a young kid, I've been involved in every level of sport. All the way up into college where I played rugby at Arizona State. Go Devils.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: What is your background?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: I have an MBA in supply chain and logistics. I worked for Avnet Electronics, which is the world's largest distributor of components. That's where I got all my hands on all this fun stuff.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Where are you guys based?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: I'm personally in Los Angeles. My co-founder is in Phoenix. He's phenomenal. We've been at this for four and a half years. We’re not a new startup, we’ve spent a lot of time thinking about this. And making sure our execution strategy is optimally...strategized.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Four and a half years seems like a while.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: I'm sorry, three and a half years.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Is it a timing issue do you think? Or has it just taken that long to come up with a product?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: It's really hard to create something tangible when you don't have any money. I don't know how to explain it. It's an iterative process. Raise money, be frugal. We've gone through two accelerator programs.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: How much have you raised to date?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: I'm coming in today with $250,000 committed to this round. We're currently raising an additional $500,000 to make it a total of $750,000,we're really looking for more than an investor. We want someone who is going to meet with us, go to our wedding, be our friends.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: That's smart.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Gotta hang out with us. Like, we know we're going to be married to these people. And so I'm here to date you guys. I want to learn about you, you guys want to learn about me. But we're really looking to selectively and strategically bring on people who we can work with for the next future.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I always tell founders that early stage investors are actually co-founders.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Right. I couldn't agree more.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Absolutely. Roll up your sleeve, dig in.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: But I’m not here to talk about me. I want to talk about the estimated 450 million athletes around the world. The Centre for Disease Control estimates that as many as 10% of those athletes - ten! - will suffer sports-related concussion at any given season. A staggering 47% of those athletes, nearly half of them who are concussed will not self-report or self-diagnose any symptoms. That means every single year, millions upon millions of individuals are remaining on the field with an unidentified or undocumented head injury. The FIT team set out to change that.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: our intelligent mouthguard, which seamlessly integrated into a standard mouth guard. This mouthguard is worn by the athlete If they are hit with a significant amount of force, this mouth guard will light up and change colors.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: I mean, like, is this... I know concussions are a problem in football.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: No, it's huge.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: Have you seen the movie?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And it's not just football. It's soccer. There are more concussions in soccer than there are in football. And now with soccer being such a huge, huge sport, I would think you would start this in soccer.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: There's so many. There's wrestling, rugby, every sport.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: And anything that's even not a contact sport. Horseback riding. Parajumping.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And just so you know, I know this space very, very well. I've sat on these boards. Um, We work a lot with concussion research at Stanford Hospital.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Dr Camarillo, very familiar.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yes. Yeah. So what a concussion basically is, all a concussion is is the inability to perform your basic functionality. That could be everything from not being able to, as you know, to focus, to just being a little bit off-center, to not being able... I mean, that is called a limited concussion, you know that.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You don't really need a mouth guard, doctors really don't need mouth guards, and especially coaches right now, if they see that you are basically unable to focus for even a spit of time right now, you are off the field and you are done. So I'm just trying to figure out where this mouth guard comes in because it's not diagnosing, right?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Nope. So first of all you made a lot of assumptions that would be great in ideal situation. someone will see that. That is a very broad assumption. When you're a volunteer football coach and you're responsible for a hundred kids that are bashing their skulls into each other two hours a day, seven days a week, statistically you will miss something. And that's what we're trying to do.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Oh this is for kids?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: This is a mass market high volume product. that anyone can afford and anyone can implement.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: But it doesn't protect them from being hurt. Because it shows after the impact has happened. It's not protecting them, at all.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: I would disagree. Because second impact syndrome is a fatal condition, in which you remain on the field with an unidentified injury, you receive a similar injury, and your brain stops working. So empirically, if we stop the second injury from happening because we got em out as soon as the first injury happened, then they are safer.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: I’m just wondering, is this the way to solve the problem? Or is helmet technology the way to solve the problem?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: I played rugby. There's no helmets in rugby.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: The data says that helmets have made things worse, right? There are more concussions post-helmets.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Helmets reduce skull force, not cranial acceleration.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Exactly, yeah.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: And it makes people reckless, right?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: It does. Moral chaos. You're more risky because you feel protected.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: I'm trying to figure out how to get down to the root of the problem. And I guess we can't solve the root of the problem, unless we just stop playing football.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Stop hitting your head against things that are hard, is the root of the problem.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Stop playing sports!

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Will you show us the mobile app and what does it do?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Of course. I'll pass this around.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Let's say this is me, I just got hit in the face.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Let's reenact it.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: There you go.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: So it's going to sync it up. You're going to download it. First your mouth guard is going to change colors if it was a significant amount of force.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: So the... The data you're receiving from the teeth or the jaw or from where? Where is it coming?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: The cranial acceleration. So how fast is the head moving in a frame of space. From the mouth guard. So what's actually measuring it. Being inside of the skull means we are physically closer, we have a better retention and coupling to the skull, so our data is just highly correlated to what the brain actually felt.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And so the coach has it on his phone, so that every time a player is hit and the mouthguard turns color, although they'll never be able to see it across a field, but it will go into his assistant coach's app or whatever and it will light up to say, number 32 should be pulled and assessed?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: I do want to clarify. So in theory that's correct, but we do not do live data transmission. Our data uses the Bluetooth protocol which has a range limitation and so that's why we have the on-device notification. So the mouth guard changes colors, come over, sync to the app, it'll sync up when you're within ten meters.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Right. Why don't you make it vibrate?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Just so you know. Those kids are never going to come in on their own.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: I'm an athlete myself, and it's very hard for someone to pull themselves out of the game. So we come into someone who has authority and says, this is our league protocol.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: But you're not going to be able to see them across a field. And they're not going to be synced up other than ten feet.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: No, no. The mouth guard will light up. And it will stay lit until it's synced back…

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But depending on who sees it, and who reacts to it.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: It stays lit until you sync it back with the base station?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Until you sync it. There's no way to hide this. You can't take your mouth guard out. Mouthguards required. In football, when I played football, every single play a ref would go around to every single kid and look at them to make sure their mouth guard was in. This was ten years ago. So I'm assuming, if they're going through that protocol, they're just checking for red lights. I mean, it’s pretty obvious if someone’s mouth is glowing red.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Is there something to turn it on?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: This is our prototype model, it doesn't work right now.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Ok got it

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: So this is a non-working prototype...

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: yeah but we’ll get to that soon enough.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: It's cheap. Initially, they're $129 to capture those early adopters. As we start to scale up, those definitely are going to come below $100.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So you're assuming that all these teams will be able to afford one of these mouth guards for every one of the players?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Like, who is going to be most receptive to getting this into the players' mouths?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: The executives in that organization. The people who make the decision with that league, because they have the most leave.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: So you're selling the league? So you want it to be mandated by the leagues?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: We are business to business. Yes.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: There seems like there's going to be some sort of rift and problem with coaches from one team to another if some of the kids have them, and some of the other kids don't. And within the team itself.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: I think it would be the opposite problem.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: That's really our marketing strategy.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: The coaches won't want the kids to have the mouth guards, because the coaches might not want to have to worry about pulling kids out of the game all the time.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay. Well that's another thing.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: It's the parents, not the schools, who would buy these mouth guards, right?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Ah. So the parents will do whatever the schools tell them to. The consumer is actually going to be the person purchasing this, but we know the decision of who and what to buy comes from a higher authority and the parents just listen to the coach.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: But he's saying the opposite. He's saying they wouldn't want to buy it because it might tell them they should be pulling the kids.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Most coaches don't want to pull the kids.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Although, these are like, I mean I'm sure these kids...

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: We're focusing on kids. Safety is more important than winning. We're not talking about professionals or D1.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Blasphemy.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: You’re right though if it’s just one kid, especially if you light up it’s not that you look geeky it’s that…

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: You're a wuss.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You're a wussy,

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: I think what you could, where you do have an angle, is selling to parents. Being like, hey, your kids need to get pulled. Otherwise, you're talking permanent brain damage.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: there's always friction when you have change.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yes, of course.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Culturally, it's coming up perfectly to our timing to enter the market where I think we're well fit with people's willingness to accept: one, wearables; two, electronics on their body; and, three, about concussions being a serious problem. And it's okay to be hurt. You're not demoralized, you're not weak. It's not your fault that you got possibly concussed. And we really are starting to see a shift in that mentality and acceptance.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: See, what you have to do is sell the parents on convincing the entire team.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yes, that's it.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Or sell the leagues.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: That's one of our strategies. That's a long-term play, is the leagues. Obviously, initially, we have early adopters, we have people who want to buy this. There's already kids who are saying this is cool, I want this. If you guys are worried about market validation, during due diligence I would be happy to show you our validation, our studies, our surveys.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: How far along are you now?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: We're doing some validation testing with Arizona State University coached by Olympic medalist Zeke Jones, who also coaches the USA freestyle team.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: How much are they paying?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: They paid like $7000 for about twenty units, because they were research grade. We're researching with the government of Japan and their Judo, they've recently mandated Judo as a requirement for high school sports, so they want to validate the riskiness of that.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: So these are all just conversations you've got going on with these folks?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: No. These are active letter of intent research programs that are ready.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So no contracts yet, right? No signed contracts?

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Here's the good news. I've already sold 5000 of them. They haven't paid for them. These are all letters of intent contingent on successful validation. That's through our beta test program, we're going to be launching first quarter 2017. We are going to be distributing in Ireland, France, Australia, Canada and New Zealand.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Cool. All right. I like seeing working prototypes, personally.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: They'll be ready in two weeks. It's not... Timing's a little off.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Yeah, well, I can't wait to see it. And then Sheel can punch me in the face and I'll see if it works.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: You can go to ASU wrestling practice, we're going to be there all season. So stop by anytime.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: you're saying all the right things, you've researched it, you have clearly the passion for this and you have three and a half years under your belt to finally make a non-working prototype, and I think the timing is right for this At this time, just because it's so early and so nebulous, and I look at that mouth guard that you showed me and I don't even really, I can't put it in my mouth, I can't feel it, I can't see it light up.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: You can put it in your mouth.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: I don't want to put it in my mouth.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: He's a germaphobe, don't you remember?

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: It's just one of my things, as an investor. I want to see something working. I want to know that you can build something that's actually functional. So I'm going to pass right now.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: So do I go?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: No, he's just one. You have to hear from all of us.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: He's just one.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Actually, I'm the only one that matters, so yeah, you can go.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Yeah. I like where you're going. I think there's a need, for something that helps save lives on the football field and other fields. I'm not, again, like Howie, I'd want to see it working. And really, it's crazy, because even if I believe you it's going to be working in two weeks, it's just something about seeing it that I think could be convincing.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: We filmed a live demo in London with the English national rugby team. It's about a five-minute video clip. It did work, it just broke. I'm not trying to excuse that. So we have video footage. Flew to London, BBC studio, filmed it all out there.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: Breaking is a concern though.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Yeah. In the mouth.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: It was the charging mechanism. No excuses. Understood.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: It's like a Samsung Galaxy Note 7, in the mouth. It's exploding. No, just kidding.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: Turn it off on the plane.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: I'm going to pass. But I think it's pretty honorable what you're doing. So that's cool.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: I'll echo what Howie said about seeing the working prototype. I think it's really hard when right now it's just a non-functional model. Even if you're only two weeks away and I don't think you'll be able to get piecemeal adoption, because I think the kids are going to rebel against it. But even if you overcome those things, and I think you can overcome those barriers, I'm a little concerned about the recurring revenue model. Because I don't think you can build a really great business on just these hardware sales. And I think that's really what you need to make this business big long term.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Right. Well, in the long term we have those things in the pipeline the permutations to make money are out there. And there's money to be spent on sports. So we're looking to capture it.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: But for now, for the product you've got, for where you're at, I think I'm going to pass.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I mean, I respect the mission, I think it's great. There is a problem out there. For me I don't feel like I can add a whole lot of value in this particular space. I'm just, it's not something that... I don't like the model. I'm not seeing the path to recurring revenue. I see hardware sales. And that's all I'm seeing right now. And so for that reason I think it's too early for me. So, I'll pass.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Okay. Cool.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Oh goodness. Okay. So, first of all what I want to say is that we so appreciated it. You’re incredibly high energy. You smile all the time. You make us feel like, we really like you. And I think it's important when you're selling something. It's all in the presentation. A lot of it is. So you should teach people how to do this.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I have a very emotional response to this. Because I've had two children that have had concussions. One is from soccer from repetitive hits, and one from football. And what I look for is something that will prevent concussions. So I do understand this would prevent the second concussion, but I'm trying to find something to invest in that would prevent the first concussion. And maybe that's just my maternal instinct connecting to this. It is too early for me, absolutely. But I do think you're onto something, and the fact that you're trying to help young people and trying to do something that we all need to be doing pro-active around concussions, good for you.

turns.speaker: Anthony
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So, I'm going to pass. But I think I'd like to see what happens when you do launch in beta.
